findings.description: Directional empirical claim ('Available evidence points toward higher food insecurity rates among gig and platform workers') presented without any citation. The epistemic flags acknowledge absent figures, but the body text asserts a directional finding without naming a source.
findings.suggestion: Either cite a specific study or survey, or reframe as 'structural conditions suggest gig workers may face elevated food insecurity' to make the inferential nature visible in body text.
findings.context: Available evidence points toward higher food insecurity rates among gig and platform workers, though systematic data remain limited -- rates appear to run above national averages...

findings.description: Date inconsistency for General Comment 19. Body text (lines 23, 39) cites 'General Comment 19 (2007)' while the epistemic flags section (line 108) cites '(2008)'. CESCR adopted GC 19 on 23 November 2007 (E/C.12/GC/19). The epistemic flag carries the incorrect year.
findings.suggestion: Change '(2008)' to '(2007)' on line 108 to match the body text and the actual adoption date.
findings.context: CESCR General Comment 19 (2008) interpretations cited from knowledge base; specific paragraph numbers have not been verified against official OHCHR text

findings.description: E-Prime violations in Developer Letter template body: 'That is not a vague aspiration -- it is a legal commitment' (line 129), 'The people building AI are not the problem. The missing framework is.' (line 131). These render as user-facing suggested text.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'That represents not a vague aspiration but a legal commitment' and 'The people building AI do not constitute the problem. The missing framework does.'
findings.context: Lines 129-131 of the Developer Letter template

findings.description: Internal cross-reference link '/blog/article-14-compulsory-primary-education' may not resolve. The target post file uses the full slug '2026-04-22-article-14-compulsory-primary-education.md'. Depending on routing configuration, the link may need the date prefix.
findings.suggestion: Verify the link resolves in the built site. If date-based slugs apply, update to match the canonical URL pattern.

findings.description: FCC broadband statistic ('approximately 14 to 17 million U.S. households') names the source type but provides no specific report, year, or dataset. The epistemic flags acknowledge this, but the body text presents a specific numeric range that warrants a concrete citation.
findings.suggestion: Add a specific FCC report citation (e.g., FCC Broadband Deployment Report [year]) with publication date, or soften to 'estimates range from...' without the specific figure.
findings.context: FCC data from recent years suggests approximately 14 to 17 million U.S. households with school-age children lack adequate broadband access, concentrated in rural areas and low-income urban neighborhoods.

findings.description: E-Prime violations in Educator Letter template: 'AI is restructuring faster than curricula adapt' (line 108), 'where the right to education is enforceable' (line 112).
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'AI restructures [the economy] faster than curricula adapt' and 'where courts can enforce the right to education.'
findings.context: Lines 108-112 of the Educator Letter template

findings.description: Inference about corporate intent stated as direct observation: 'private economic benefit drives the purpose' and 'platform efficiency drives the purpose.' Fair witness discipline requires distinguishing observable effects from inferred purpose.
findings.suggestion: Reframe as observable outcomes: 'the observable effect reduces labor costs and expands margins' rather than asserting what 'drives' the purpose.
findings.context: When platform companies classify workers as independent contractors to reduce labor costs and expand margins, private economic benefit drives the purpose.

findings.description: Unattributed 'research suggests it does not fall evenly' claim. The Article 2 post cites Frey & Osborne (2017) and Autor (2015) for the same underlying claim, but this post leaves the research unattributed.
findings.suggestion: Add citation inline matching the Article 2 post: '(Frey & Osborne, 2017; Autor, 2015)' or similar.
findings.context: If AI displacement falls disproportionately on workers by age, race, or gender -- and research suggests it does not fall evenly -- states have a specific obligation...

findings.description: Citation scope mismatch: cites Frey & Osborne (2017) and Autor (2015) for occupational automation risk, then extends the claim to demographic concentration without a source that directly establishes that link. The interpretive step presents as documented finding.
findings.suggestion: Either cite a study that directly connects automation risk to demographic patterns (e.g., Muro, Maxim & Whiton, 2019, Brookings) or add hedging before the demographic claim.
findings.context: Research on labor market automation risk (Frey & Osborne, 2017; Autor, 2015) suggests that displacement does not distribute randomly; it concentrates in occupational profiles that correspond, by documented historical contingency, to specific demographic groups.

findings.description: Central automation claim ('AI automation could affect a substantial share of current work activities within a decade') lacks any specific citation. Multiple studies have published varying estimates. The hedging language meets fair-witness minimum but a claim this central warrants at least one named source.
findings.suggestion: Add a parenthetical citation to at least one published labor economics study (e.g., McKinsey Global Institute, Goldman Sachs, or Acemoglu & Restrepo).
findings.context: Research suggests AI automation could affect a substantial share of current work activities within a decade, with administrative, customer service, and lower-wage service roles among the most exposed.

epistemic_flags: E-Prime scan relies on pattern matching -- context-dependent 'to be' forms in quotations or proper names may produce false positives or false negatives
Fair witness confidence scores reflect scanner judgment, not ground truth -- borderline cases (0.70-0.80) carry higher uncertainty
Cross-reference link resolution (f4) depends on build-time routing configuration not inspected during this scan
